q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way in which industrialization has affected the environment since 1900.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of accelerated environmental damage in the twentieth century, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which international responses to environmental problems have been limited.

sample_answers.a: The burning of fossil fuels for industry, transport, and electricity has released vast quantities of carbon dioxide, raising atmospheric CO2 from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 ppm today and driving global warming.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the twentieth century's unprecedented population growth and industrial output multiplied humanity's demands on nature: more people consuming more energy, more goods, and more land inevitably produced more pollution, deforestation, and waste.
sample_answers.c: Because the worst polluters (industrialized nations) and the most vulnerable victims (poor countries) are different, and because cutting emissions imposes immediate economic costs for distant future benefits, nations have repeatedly failed to agree on binding reductions.

q1.stimulus:
Historians describe the twentieth century as the period when human activity became a geological force. Industrialization, which had already transformed landscapes in the nineteenth century, accelerated to an unprecedented scale: global population quadrupled, energy use multiplied, and synthetic chemicals, plastics, and nuclear materials introduced pollutants that nature had never encountered. The most far-reaching change was invisible — the accumulation of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels, which began altering the planet's climate. By the century's end, scientists could measure the transformation precisely: carbon dioxide concentrations, stable for millennia, were rising year after year. Yet the political response lagged far behind the science, as the costs of action fell on the present while the worst consequences lay in the future.
—Historian's account of environmental change in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE effect of pesticides described by Carson.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which Carson's book changed public attitudes toward the environment.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why chemical companies attacked Carson's findings.

sample_answers.a: Carson describes how pesticides like DDT accumulate in food chains, killing birds and wildlife far from where they were sprayed and threatening human health through contaminated food and water.
sample_answers.b: By documenting the hidden dangers of chemicals that people had assumed were safe, she made millions of readers question industrial progress and helped launch the modern environmental movement.
sample_answers.c: Her findings threatened a multi-billion-dollar industry; if the public accepted that pesticides were dangerous, companies faced regulation, lawsuits, and lost sales, so they sought to discredit her as hysterical and unscientific.

q2.stimulus:
The chemicals to which life is asked to make its adjustment are no longer merely the calcium and silica and copper and all the rest of the minerals washed out of the rocks and carried in rivers to the sea; they are the synthetic creations of man's inventive mind, brewed in his laboratories, and having no counterparts in nature. ... To have risked so much in our efforts to mold nature to our satisfaction and yet to have failed in achieving our goal would indeed be the final irony. These sprays, dusts, and aerosols are now applied almost universally to farms, gardens, forests, and homes — nonselective chemicals that have the power to kill every insect, the 'good' and the 'bad.'
—Adapted from Rachel Carson, Silent Spring, 1962

q3.directions: Use the chart below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE trend shown in the Keeling Curve.
parts.b: Explain ONE human cause of the trend shown in the chart.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why the Keeling Curve became important evidence in debates about climate change.

sample_answers.a: The chart shows atmospheric carbon dioxide rising steadily from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to over 420 ppm in recent years, with a repeating annual up-and-down cycle superimposed on the long-term climb.
sample_answers.b: The rise is caused primarily by burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) for energy, industry, and transport, which releases carbon stored underground over millions of years into the atmosphere in a geological instant.
sample_answers.c: Because it provided direct, continuous measurements (rather than theory or models) showing CO2 accumulating year after year, the curve gave scientists undeniable physical evidence that human activity was changing the atmosphere — evidence that could not be dismissed as speculation.

q3.stimulus: The chart is the Keeling Curve, showing monthly mean concentrations of atmospheric carbon dioxide measured at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii from 1958 to the present. The data, collected by Charles David Keeling and continued by NOAA and the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, is the longest continuous record of atmospheric CO2. The curve shows a steady rise from about 315 parts per million when measurements began, with small seasonal oscillations caused by Northern Hemisphere plant growth.
